prompt_version: s5-extract-facts-v2 (adapted from Paleo Atlas extract-facts-v3; v2 after Sofía's S5 review)

facts.statement: The research investigated if existing aircraft seat safety tests give enough data to know if passengers can evacuate safely after an emergency landing.
facts.subject: other

facts.statement: The study involved 17 dynamic lab tests on economy-class seats using Hybrid II crash test dummies.
facts.subject: other

facts.statement: Two impact scenarios were tested: hitting a bulkhead and hitting the seat in the row in front.
facts.subject: other

facts.statement: Researchers measured head injury criteria, head accelerations, and where the head hit to evaluate the risk of brain injury and fainting.
facts.subject: other

facts.statement: Tests involving bulkhead impacts more often went over the acceptable head injury threshold of 1,000, suggesting a higher risk of severe brain injury.
facts.subject: other

facts.statement: Impacts against the seat in the row ahead showed lower risk levels than bulkhead impacts.
facts.subject: other

facts.statement: A larger distance between seat rows (pitch) was a protective factor, with head injury values dropping significantly when the pitch was greater than 35 inches.
facts.subject: other

facts.statement: The front of the head was the most common impact zone, occurring in 91% of the cases.
facts.subject: other

facts.statement: The study recommends adding rotational acceleration criteria, testing diverse groups like children and the elderly, and including seat pitch in safety standards.
facts.subject: other
